rv.q: Mark Bell's direction keeps an unrelenting pace that leaves the audience breathless and the actors clueless.
For much of the night, you feel like you are watching the luckiest Broadway imposters in the world, and you probably are.
“That Goes Wrong,” the winner of London’s Olivier for best comedy, finds the line that separates the annoying and stupid from the I-can’t-believe-I’m-laughing-at-this brilliance.
It’s so ridiculous it makes you feel almost ashamed to love it.
The show is pure comedic eye candy, and technically flawless.
Though it could benefit from some cutting, the production is an idiot's delight.

An overabundance of non-sensical sight gags, slow burns, pratfalls, missed cues, wink-winks and the like dull the viewer’s senses and drag out a sophomoric sketch that would be sharper and funnier at an intermissionless 80 minutes.
Everything is pitched so aggressively, you wind up feeling as battered as the ensemble.
Depending on your tolerance for ceaseless slapstick, The Play That Goes Wrong will either have you rolling in the aisles or rolling your eyes.
Long before the red herrings had been sorted out I came to feel that it wasn’t just the play-within-the-play that was going wrong, but the whole exhausting, exhausted conceit.
But for all the strenuous effort involved, the repetitive show evaporates in your mind the moment it concludes.
Without a doubt, "The Play That Goes Wrong" is the funniest play Broadway has ever seen.
The delightfully entertaining farce is easily the funniest play I've ever seen.
All told, The Play That Goes Wrong goes uproariously right.
The form, as the riotous British transplant The Play That Goes Wrong shows, written by cast members Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, and Henry Shields, is ripe for satire.
What an achievement to pull it off so well, and so consistently.
Under Mark Bell's inspired staging, everything works to make it seem like nothing's working, including a truly remarkable set.
In the end, and basically throughout, The Play that Goes Wrong has gone very right, indeed.
The eight performers have individual personalities but come together to form a tight ensemble well-disciplined in the art of being hilariously bad.
The laughs are non-stop and most of them are really cheap.
That Goes Wrong is just right: A ridiculously entertaining disaster.
This is two hours of unapologetic, stupid fun, buoyed along by a cast of ultra-committed performers.

For much of its two-hour running time, “The Play That Goes Wrong” offers a hilarious tribute to the spirit of the theater and the mantra that the show must go on — served up with a thick slice of ham.

Audiences may indeed enjoy The Play That Goes Wrong….if not as much as Hamilton, perhaps, surely as much as Noises Off, which it resembles, minus the plates of sardines nor anything approaching that play’s cleverness.
You would think this one-joke premise would run out steam after an hour, but Mark Bell’s breakneck staging keep the guffaws building and as the play-within-a-play keeps deteriorating.
You can, nevertheless, absolutely expect to laugh, even if perhaps not as often or as hard as that person next to you.
Ultimately, though, it's not much more than an elaborate parlor trick.
The effort here is pure slapstick from the very first moment to the eventual fadeout, and over a two hour-plus running time the repetitive conceit becomes preciously thin.
Cumulatively, it's farce on steroids, without any brains.
The pace is so relentless and the absence of anything but gags, gags, gags quickly wore out its welcome.
As things stand, for me at least, a comedy this tired just can’t be right.
They simply do the play very well.
A comedy that comes up short with laughs and overstays its welcome — now that’s murder.
The result is an uproarious theatrical experience unlike any other – and one that will have you laughing until your sides ache.
Instead, sit back and marvel at the mischief-making of the Mischief Theatre company, whose skills in physical comedy and split-second timing are impeccable.
Our British cousins have always favored farce, more than we do over here, and when served up as expertly as this, we can understand why.
Without a dull unfunny moment in this two hour production, I’d say it’s quite an achievement, one that even on second viewing, kept me laughing from the first second to the last.
The Play that Goes Wrong is laugh–out–loud funny, even for me.
I was uninhibitedly laughing aloud through much of the mayhem created on stage by this superb gang of actors.
Although I already saw it in London, I laughed as much this time as I did last time.
Something as silly as this could only work if it was put together with serious craft, and it was, like a pristinely assembled jigsaw puzzle that, when put together, makes you scream with laughter.

It’s one sight gag after another as things collapse on the fireplace mantel, necessitating the stage manager Annie (Bryony Corrigan) to physically throw her arms through holes to hold things up, and more.

Under Mark Bell’s direction, the ensemble cast delivers a high-energy, brilliantly acted farce that celebrates the magic of the theatre by highlighting its foibles – a resplendent conception concocted by writers Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer and Henry Shields.
There is NOTHING wrong with The Play That Goes Wrong.
Despite its few missteps, anyone who enjoys farce will be smiling, chuckling or laughing the entire evening.
But if all you’re looking for is a chance to laugh, loudly and often, The Play That Goes Wrong may be your best bet of the season.
Overall, The Play that Goes Wrong is exactly what you expect it to be: something very funny, but ultimately predictable.
At the end of the day, there aren’t nearly enough revivals of Noises Off or The Real Inspector Hound to justify this cheap and disappointing imitation.
It is deserving of all of the adjectives listed above.
Two plus hours of repetitive slapstick without much plot or any wit is more than I can enjoy.

aw.sub: Won Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Critics find this British farce about a disastrous amateur production mostly amusing, praising the cast's expert physical comedy and precise slapstick execution, though some dismiss it as a one-joke premise that wears thin.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
